hints: Think about what causes limewater to turn milky, which white solid is forming from soluble $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Picture the milky change**
Limewater starts as a clear, colourless solution of $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$. When $\text{CO}_2$ bubbles through, it turns milky white. That milkiness is tiny solid particles of calcium carbonate, $\text{CaCO}_3$, suspended in water.

Balance the atoms**
You are joining $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $2\text{OH}^-$ with $\text{CO}_2$ to make $\text{CaCO}_3$ and water. One $\text{CO}_2$ supplies the $\text{CO}_3$ unit and one $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ balances H and O: $\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \longrightarrow \text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Remember the visible test depends on starting with a clear solution and forming an insoluble white solid on adding $\text{CO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Link the test to solubility**
A good test needs two things. Start with dissolved hydroxide ions in a clear solution, then make an insoluble carbonate that you can see as a white precipitate.

Apply to barium**
Like $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble enough to give $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)$ and $\text{OH}^-(aq)$. With $\text{CO}_2$ it forms barium carbonate, $\text{BaCO}_3$, which is insoluble, so you still get the milky white precipitate.
Final answer: $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble enough to give a clear solution and $\text{BaCO}_3$ is insoluble, so a white precipitate forms with $\text{CO}_2$.

hints: Compare the solubility of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ with $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ and think how much dissolved $\text{OH}^-$ is available to react.
Think about whether the possible product $\text{MgCO}_3$ would appear as a white precipitate or stay dissolved.
walkthrough:
Spot the problem with the starting solution**
Solubility of hydroxides increases down Group 2, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ at the top is essentially insoluble in water. A saturated solution contains almost no $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)$ and $\text{OH}^-(aq)$, so there is hardly anything for $\text{CO}_2$ to react with.

Spot the problem with the product**
Even if a little reaction occurred, magnesium carbonate, $\text{MgCO}_3$, is soluble, unlike $\text{CaCO}_3$ and $\text{BaCO}_3$. With no insoluble white solid forming, you would see no milky change, so the test fails.

Final answer: $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble / very sparingly soluble, so very little dissolved hydroxide is present.
No precipitate of $\text{MgCO}_3$ forms as $\text{MgCO}_3$ is soluble, so no milky appearance is seen.

hints: Recall which carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature, $\text{MgCO}_3$ or $\text{BaCO}_3$, to state the stability trend down Group 2.
Compare the ionic radius and charge density of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, both have 2+ charge but very different size.
Think how a small, highly polarising cation distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion and weakens a C-O bond to release $\text{CO}_2$.
walkthrough:
State the observed trend**
$\text{MgCO}_3$ decomposes on gentle heating while $\text{BaCO}_3$ needs very strong heating. Stability to heat increases going down Group 2: $\text{MgCO}_3 < \text{CaCO}_3 < \text{SrCO}_3 < \text{BaCO}_3$.

Compare the cations**
All the cations are $2+$, but size grows down the group. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is tiny with a very high charge density, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large with a low charge density. High charge density means strong polarising power.

Explain distortion of carbonate**
Picture $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ as a central C bonded to three O atoms. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulls strongly on the electron cloud of a neighbouring oxygen, distorting the ion. This polarisation weakens a C-O bond and makes it easy to break to give $\text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ much less, so the carbonate survives to higher temperature.

Final answer: Thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
Cationic radius increases down the group, so charge density decreases.
Larger cations polarise the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion less, so the C-O bond is less weakened and more heat is needed to decompose the carbonate.

hints: Look up the ionic radii of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ in the Data Booklet and decide which ion is smaller and more polarising.
Apply the same polarisation argument as for Group 2 to predict which carbonate, $\text{NiCO}_3$ or $\text{CaCO}_3$, needs less heat to decompose.
walkthrough:
Pull out the data**
From the Data Booklet, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ has radius about $0.070\,\text{nm}$ while $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has radius about $0.099\,\text{nm}$. Both ions carry the same $2+$ charge, so size alone controls polarising power.

Predict the stability**
Smaller $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ has higher charge density, so it polarises and distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion more strongly than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ does. That extra distortion weakens the carbonate, so $\text{NiCO}_3$ breaks down to $\text{NiO} + \text{CO}_2$ more easily, meaning it decomposes more readily than $\text{CaCO}_3$.

Final answer: Radius of $\text{Ni}^{2+} = 0.070\,\text{nm}$, radius of $\text{Ca}^{2+} = 0.099\,\text{nm}$.
$\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is smaller and more polarising, so $\text{NiCO}_3$ decomposes more readily (at lower temperature) than $\text{CaCO}_3$.
